newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade bourse turnover down in week to Dec 27.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade bourse turnover down in week to Dec 27.

text.p: The Belgrade Stock Exchange (BSE) reported on Monday a 10.9 percent fall in turnover during the week ending December 27.
Traders blamed tightening liquidity in the banking sector for the decline.
Total turnover fell for the second consecutive week and stood at 23.13 million dinars ($4.51 million) in 148 deals, down from 25.96 million dinars in 171 transactions a week ago.
Traders said the end of last week was marked by massive withdrawal of funds, with banks and companies preparing to pay pensions, wages and other overdue liabilities before the end of the year.
"The scene becomes horrible. There is no fresh money and everybody seems to be trying to collect from debtors," one trader told Reuters.

More than 100 Yugoslav banks received a first blow when the National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) introduced a reserve requirement early in September in order to regulate surging liquidity of the banking sector.
Then, two weeks ago, the NBY called on commercial banks licenced for foreign exchange operations abroad to deposit additional funds to retain their licences.
Depending on the licence, banks were required to deposit one to two million U.S. dollars as a permanent deposit with the NBY carrying an annual interest rate equal to LIBOR.
Half of the sum was to be paid by December 25 and the remainder by January 15 to the account of the London-based Anglo-Yugoslav bank.
Economists said the decision was motivated by central bank attempts to beef up its scarce hard currency reserves.
Analysts also saw the decision as a means of cleansing the oversized banking sector of insolvent and inefficient banks.
They also said Anglo-Yugoslav bank needed fresh capital by December 30 to have its licence renewed.
"With the crisis of the Yugoslav banking sector obviously deepening, we cannot hope for any better performance by the local financial market any time soon," one dealer said.
According to the Accounting and Payments Operations Office, the accounts of 11 Yugoslav banks were in the red on Monday.
For the week ending December 27, the BSE reported the following details:
* Commercial paper accounted for 122 deals worth 16.733 million dinars.
* Treasury bills traded 19 times for a volume of 1.509 million dinars.
Interest rates on commercial paper and treasury bills ranged between an annual 331 and 793 percent.
* The central bank short-term bonds saw one deal worth three million dinars.
* The bourse reported two transactions in wheat selling contracts worth 1.628 million dinars. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
